head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sorted prize positions (the input is sorted)
A segment of length `k` covers a window of consecutive prizes
Left end of the window of prizes within distance `k` of `p[i]`, found with two pointers
Prizes in the best segment that ENDS at prize `i`
The most prizes one segment can collect among the first `x` prizes
Prefix maximum, so a second segment can use everything to the left
Second segment ends at `i`; the first segment is the best one entirely before index `j` (no overlap)
Update the prefix maximum with the window ending at `i`

blocks.h: Why a prefix maximum and a window?
p: Two segments that do not overlap can be separated by a split point. For the segment ending at `i`, the other segment must lie entirely to the left of the window start `j`, and the best such segment is `best[j]`. Computing the prefix maximum once avoids trying every pair of windows (O(n²)).

2555.takeaway: Two non-overlapping segments: slide a window of prizes within distance k and combine it with the best window entirely to its left (prefix maximum).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `cnt[v]` = how many more copies of `v` basket 1 has than basket 2 (can be negative)
`Counter.subtract` keeps zero and negative counts, unlike the `-` operator
An odd difference means the fruit can't be split evenly between the baskets: answer −1
Each surplus value `v` must move `|c| / 2` copies across; this collects the values to be swapped
Of the `len(extra)` fruits that must move, only half the swaps are needed; pair the smallest half with the largest half, paying the smaller one's cost
Each swap costs the cheaper fruit
A swap costs `x` directly, or `2 · m` via the globally cheapest fruit `m` (swap it in and back out)

blocks.p: Value `2` has two extra copies in basket 1 and value `1` has two extra copies in basket 2 (differences `{4: 0, 2: 2, 1: -2}`), so one `1` and one `2` must change baskets. The fruits to move are [1, 2]. The globally cheapest fruit costs 1, so the swap costs `min(x, 2·1)` and the total is 1.

blocks.h: Why only the smaller half of `extra` pays?
p: Each swap exchanges one fruit from basket 1 with one from basket 2. The cost is the smaller of the two swapped fruits, so we always pair the smallest unmatched fruit with the largest. Going through the sorted list, the cheaper half of the list is exactly the set of costs paid.

2561.takeaway: Rearranging fruits: halve the count imbalance to find the fruits that must move, sort them, and pay min(cost, 2 × global minimum) for the cheaper half.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Give every child $1 first; to reach $8 a child needs 7 more
How many children can reach exactly $8 (each needs $7 more)
Greedy: maximise the number of $8 children
Everyone has $8 but there is money left over: someone would exceed $8, so one child must drop out of the $8 group
The only remaining child would get exactly $4 (1 + 3), which is forbidden

p: The rules say nobody may get $4, and every dollar must be given out. After handing out as many $8s as possible, leftover money must go to non-$8 children. If there is no such child, or the single remaining child would end up with $4, the only fix is to take one child out of the $8 group, which makes room.

head: Situation
Fix
rows: all children at $8 and money left

2591.takeaway: Maximum children with exactly $8: give $1 to each, hand out groups of $7 greedily, then fix the two corner cases (leftover money with no free child, or a forbidden $4).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Degree of each node and the set of nodes not yet removed
A leaf with no coin is useless to visit, so delete it; its parent may then become a coinless leaf, so repeat
Remove subtrees that contain no coins
`for _ in range(2)`: remove all current leaves

The robot collects coins within distance 2 of where it stands, so a leaf with a coin can be reached from 2 edges away; peeling the leaves twice shrinks the tree to the part the robot must actually walk
A walk that starts and ends at the same node and visits every remaining node traverses each remaining edge twice; a tree with `v` nodes has `v − 1` edges
If everything was peeled away, no walking is needed

p: A path of 6 nodes, coins at the two ends: `[1,0,0,0,0,1]`.

head: Stage
Nodes still alive
rows: after removing coinless leaves (none: both ends have coins)
after peeling leaves a second time

p: 2 nodes remain, so the robot walks 1 edge(s) twice: 2.

From a node the robot gathers every coin within distance 2. A coin on a leaf is collected by standing at the leaf's grandparent, so the leaf and its parent never need to be visited. Peeling two layers of leaves removes precisely those nodes. The remaining tree is the minimal connected set the robot must tour.

head: Approach
Time
rows: try every start with a full DFS (Depth-First Search)

2603.takeaway: Collect coins in a tree: delete coinless leaves, then peel two more layers of leaves (coins within distance 2 are free); the answer is twice the remaining edge count.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The decimal text of the number, including a leading `-` for negatives
The width includes the minus sign
outer loop over columns `j`, inner over rows `i`
Column-major scan so we can keep the maximum of one column at a time

p: The minus sign takes one character, so `-15` needs 3 characters while `15` needs 2. Converting to a string counts exactly the characters that would be printed.
`[max(len(str(x)) for x in col) for col in zip(*grid)]` does the same in one line: `zip(*grid)` transposes the rows into columns.

2639.takeaway: Column widths: the maximum string length of the numbers in each column (negatives count the minus sign).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of copies of `"abc"` needed so the word can be a subsequence-compatible sequence of `abc` blocks
If the next letter is not strictly greater, it cannot belong to the same `abc` block, so it starts a new one
A strictly increasing run fits within one block
The final string has `3 · groups` characters; we keep `len(word)` of them, so the rest are inserted

p: A valid string is `abcabc…`. Inside one `abc` block letters strictly increase, so the word splits into maximal strictly increasing runs, each needing its own block. A drop or repeat (`b <= a`) marks the boundary between runs.

2645.takeaway: Minimum additions to make 'abc'-repeated string: split the word into strictly increasing runs; each run needs one 'abc' block, so the answer is 3 × runs − length.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each value has been seen across BOTH prefixes
Arrays are permutations, so each value appears at most once in each
The value is now present in both prefixes: it is common
A count of 2 means seen in A and in B
One more value common to both prefixes
Prefix common count after this index

p: Each value appears once in `A` and once in `B`. The first time a value shows up in either prefix its count becomes 1; when it appears in the other prefix its count becomes 2 and it is common from then on. Counting how many values reach 2 gives the answer without comparing prefixes.

head: Approach
Time
rows: intersect the prefixes at every index

2657.takeaway: Prefix common array: one Counter over both arrays; a value reaching count 2 becomes common, and the running total is the answer at each index.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Subtract the pairs that involve the OLD colour of `idx` (only if `idx` was coloured and a neighbour matches it)
Add the pairs that involve the NEW colour
A change at `idx` can only affect pairs `(idx − 1, idx)` and `(idx, idx + 1)`

blocks.h: Why subtract before and add after?
p: Recolouring changes only the pairs touching `idx`. The code first removes the pairs that existed with the old colour, then adds the pairs that exist with the new colour. Recomputing all pairs would cost O(n) per query.

head: Approach
Time per query
rows: adjust the two neighbouring pairs (this code)

2672.takeaway: Adjacent equal colours: keep a running pair count; before recolouring subtract the pairs with the old colour, after recolouring add the pairs with the new one (only two neighbours).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Shortest distance to node `u` having used exactly `h` hops (edges whose weight is set to 0)
Dijkstra with a resource in the state: (node, hops used)
Dijkstra's algorithm (shortest paths with non-negative weights)
Walk the edge normally and pay its weight
Use a hop: the edge costs 0, so the cost stays `c` and the hop count rises
Best over every hop count used at the destination

p: Edges `0-1 (4)`, `0-2 (2)`, `2-3 (6)`; from 1 to 3 with `k = 2` hops. Final table `dist[node][hops used]` (∞ = unreachable):
The best distance to node 3 is 2: hop over `1→0` (free) and walk `0→2` (2), then hop over `2→3` (free).

blocks.h: Why add the hops to the state?
p: The best route to a node may depend on how many free edges are left. A plain per-node distance would discard a costlier route that saved a hop. With states (node, hops used), each is optimal for its own budget.

2714.takeaway: Shortest path with k free hops: Dijkstra over (node, hops used) states, where an edge is either paid for or used as a free hop.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: a 2×2 block is named by its top-left corner `(a, b)`
`for a in (x - 1, x): for b in (y - 1, y)`
A black cell `(x, y)` lies in the up-to-four blocks whose top-left corner is `(x−1 or x, y−1 or y)`
Each cell belongs to at most 4 blocks
Keep only corners that actually name a block
Number of black cells in block `(a, b)`; only blocks that contain at least one black cell are stored
Blocks with zero black cells are all the rest
Counts by complement (the grid can be 10^5 wide, so don't enumerate)

p: `m = 3`, `n = 3`, black cell `(0, 0)`: it lies only in the block whose top-left corner is `(0, 0)` (the other corners fall outside).

blocks.h: Why count only blocks that contain black cells?
p: The grid can be 10⁵ × 10⁵, but there are at most 4 blocks per black cell. Storing counts for those blocks in a dictionary uses O(black cells) memory; the number of empty blocks follows from the total number of blocks minus the others.

2768.takeaway: Black blocks: count, per 2×2 block touched by a black cell, how many black cells it holds; blocks with zero are the total minus the rest.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the longest non-decreasing subarray ending at index `i` if `nums1[i]` is chosen at `i`
Dynamic Programming (DP) with two choices per position
The new values for index `i + 1`; computed from the old `a1`, `a2` (so the update uses old values)
Compute into new variables, then assign
Extend a chain ending in `nums1[i-1]` or `nums2[i-1]` by either `nums1[i]` or `nums2[i]` when it stays non-decreasing
All four combinations (previous choice × current choice)

p: At each position we may take the value from either array, and the next position's validity depends on which value was taken. So the DP keeps the best run length for each choice, and each transition checks the four possible predecessor/current pairs.

2771.takeaway: Longest non-decreasing subarray from two arrays: DP with two states per index (value taken from nums1 or nums2), extending from either previous state when the order holds.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The first character of each word (a generator expression)
Collect one element from each item
Concatenate the first letters into a string
Compare with the target; strings of different lengths are automatically unequal

p: `words = ['alice','bob','charlie']`, `s = 'abc'`:
The first letters join to `abc`, which equals `s`, so the answer is True.
If the number of words differs from `len(s)`, the joined string has a different length, and `==` returns False. The comparison covers both the letters and the length in one step.

bullets: Space: O(number of words) for the joined string.

2828.takeaway: Acronym check: join the first letters of the words and compare with s.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Horizontal and vertical distance to the target
Chebyshev distance setting: a king-like move changes both coordinates by at most 1 per second
The fastest possible walk takes `max(dx, dy)` seconds (diagonal steps cover both axes at once); any extra time can be burned by moving back and forth or around
If we start on the target, we can stay (t = 0) or burn time, except for exactly 1 second since we MUST move each second and cannot return in one step

blocks.h: Why can extra time always be burned?
p: You must move every second, and you may step to any of the 8 neighbours. If you are not at the target, you can waste a second by stepping to a neighbour and back or moving around, so any `t ≥ max(dx, dy)` works. At the target itself, a single second is impossible (you'd have to leave and can't be back), but two or more seconds work (step out and back).

2849.takeaway: Reachable at time t with 8-direction moves: Chebyshev distance max(dx, dy) ≤ t, except that standing on the target for exactly 1 second is impossible.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Each directed edge `u → v` is stored both ways: walking it forward costs 0, walking it backward costs 1 reversal
Treat the directed graph as undirected with a cost for going against the arrow
`total` = reversals needed so that every node is reachable from node 0
second traversal: `ans[v] = ans[u] + (1 if w == 0 else -1)`
Moving the root from `u` to `v`: if the edge `u → v` points away from `u` (cost 0 from `u`), it must now be reversed (+1); if it pointed toward `u`, reversing it is no longer needed (−1)
Rerooting: update the answer in O(1) from the neighbour's answer
An iterative stack and queue avoid Python's recursion limit on deep trees

p: `n = 4`, edges `2→0`, `2→1`, `1→3`: the answer for each starting node.

Computing the answer from scratch for each node costs O(n) each, O(n²) in total. Moving the root across one edge changes the answer by exactly ±1 (the orientation of that single edge), so after one initial pass we can fill every other node in O(1) using its neighbour's answer.

2858.takeaway: Edge reversals so every node is reachable: compute the cost for root 0, then reroot along each edge with ±1.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Try each machine separately: all alloys must come from ONE machine
Can we make `a` alloys on this machine within the budget?
Metal `j` needed is `a · comp[j]`; we already hold `stock[j]`, so buy only the shortfall at `cost[j]` each
`ok` is monotone: if `a` alloys are affordable, so are fewer
Upper midpoint when the feasible branch keeps `mid`

p: Budget 15, empty stock, metal costs `[1,2,3]`, two machines:

The total cost grows with the number of alloys, so affordability is True…True False…False. Binary search finds the largest affordable count in O(log(budget)) checks, each O(n). Trying counts one by one would be O(budget · n).

2861.takeaway: Maximum alloys: for each machine binary search the largest count whose shortfall (needed minus stock) costs at most the budget; take the best machine.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Ways to be AT the destination after the moves so far
State by relationship to the destination
Ways to be in the destination's ROW but at a different column
Ways to be in the destination's COLUMN but at a different row
Ways to be in a cell sharing neither row nor column
the tuple assignment with four formulas

Each move changes the row or the column to ANY other value; the formulas count how many cells of each class are reachable from each class (for example from the destination, `m − 1` cells in the same row and `n − 1` in the same column)
Group symmetrical cells into four classes instead of tracking n·m cells
Put the 1 in the class that describes the starting cell

p: `n = 3` rows, `m = 2` columns, `k = 2` moves, source `(1,1)`, destination `(2,2)`: they differ in both row and column, so the start is class O.

A move changes either the row or the column to a different value. Whether a cell is the destination, shares its row, shares its column, or neither fully determines how many ways it can reach each class next, so cells in the same class are interchangeable. That collapses an n·m-state DP (Dynamic Programming) into 4 states and k steps, giving O(k).

2912.takeaway: Ways to reach a cell with exactly k row-or-column moves: classify cells relative to the destination (at it, same row, same column, other) and run a 4-state transition k times.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the longest subsequence of the numbers processed so far whose sum is EXACTLY `s`; `−∞` if impossible
0/1 knapsack where the value is the item count
The empty subsequence has sum 0 and length 0
Go from large sums to small so each number is used at most once
Take `x`: the best subsequence for `s − x` plus one more element
Marks unreachable sums so they never win a comparison
If the target is unreachable (still `−∞`) return −1

p: `nums = [1,2,3,4,5]`, `target = 9`: `dp[0..9]` after each number.

Going from high sums to low sums means `dp[s − x]` still holds the value from BEFORE the current number was considered, so the number is used once. Iterating upward would let one number be added repeatedly (unbounded knapsack).

head: Direction
Meaning
rows: each number any number of times

2915.takeaway: Longest subsequence with a target sum: 0/1 knapsack where dp[s] is the maximum count achieving sum s, iterating sums downward.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of zeros in each array; each zero must become a positive integer, so at least 1
The smallest possible sum of array 1: every zero becomes 1
Array 1 is the smaller side but has no zeros to increase: it can never reach `b`
Otherwise the smaller array can raise its zeros to match the larger array's minimum sum

blocks.h: Why is the answer the maximum of the two lower bounds?
p: Each array's sum is at least its all-ones minimum. The target equal sum must be at least the larger minimum. The array with the smaller minimum can reach it by increasing any of its zeros, but only if it HAS a zero; otherwise its sum is stuck below the target and the answer is −1.

2918.takeaway: Equal sums after replacing zeros: each array's minimum sum treats every zero as 1; the answer is the larger minimum unless the smaller one has no zero to grow.
